text.text: You're sitting in a small classroom with Katya, your advisor. Today she is giving a lesson on what she calls the Voice of Fire.
> look at the board
The board is blank. On a shelf beside it are the rolled boards of past lessons; one is labelled The Pillaging.
> remember the Pillaging
Someone lives in their home.
> live in your home
You live in your home, as you always have.
The Pillager enters their home.
> enter their home
You enter their home.
The Pillager takes things from their home.
> take things from their home
You take what you want from their home, and leave.
> listen
"It's a pattern in abstract phenomenology," she explains. "We'll start with a basic example."
She starts by writing a series of statements on the chalkboard:
the Voice of Fire
The laying of the tinder
The laying of the kindling over the tinder
The stacking of the firewood over the kindling
The sparking of the tinder, creating an ember
The spreading of the ember to the kindling, creating a flame
The spreading of the flame to the firewood, creating a blaze
The consumption of all within the blaze
The ash left behind

text.text: The laying of the tinder (cut at top)
> lay the tinder
A small patch of tinder is placed in the hearth.
The laying of the kindling over the tinder
> lay the kindling
A layer of kindling is added over the tinder.
The stacking of the firewood over the kindling
> stack the firewood
Logs of firewood are stacked systematically over the kindling.
The sparking of the tinder, creating an ember
> spark the tinder
A single spark is added to the tinder. It catches and forms an ember.
The spreading of the ember to the kindling, creating a flame
> spread to the kindling
The ember glows, spreading to the kindling above. The kindling is acquired by a growing flame.
The spreading of the flame to the firewood, creating a blaze
> spread to the firewood
The flame grows, and reaches the firewood, setting it alight. The blaze glows, feeding on the wooden fuel.
The consumption of all within the blaze
> burn
The blaze continues to spread through the logs, arranged perfectly to give themselves up to the burning. The hearth burns bright and hot, for a time.
The ash left behind
> reduce to ash
As the wooden fuel is spent, the blaze dies down, gradually dwindling to nothing. A pile of black ash is left behind in the hearth.
> remember the Voice of Fire
The laying of the tinder
The laying of the kindling over the tinder
The stacking of the firewood over the kindling
The sparking of the tinder, creating an ember
The spreading of the ember to the kindling, creating a flame

"Now," she says. "Consider this story:"
A group of friends takes a weekend trip to camp in the woods.
As it darkens outside, they gather tinder, kindling and firewood.
They dig a pit in the ground.
They lay the tinder in the middle of the pit.
They pile the kindling on over it.
They stack the logs in layers over the kindling.
One of them lights a match, and carefully touches its flame to the tinder.
The fire starts, spreading first to the kindling and then the logs.
The group begins to sing an old song together.
The fire burns brightly for awhile, and the friends tend to it, adding more logs periodically, as they continue to sing and tell stories.
As it grows late, they stop adding wood, and the flame dwindles. The friends retreat to their tents.
The remaining embers fizzle out, leaving behind ash.

text.text: > speak as the friends
You speak as the friends.
> travel to the woods
You all make your way out of town, in cars piled full of food, tents and musical instruments.
You arrive at the campground in the woods.
> gather tinder, kindling and firewood
As it begins to grow dark, your group searches for and finds: - tinder - kindling - firewood
> dig a pit in the ground
You dig a pit, a foot deep and 3 feet in diameter.
> lay the tinder in the pit
You place a patch of fluffy tinder in the pit.
> pile the kindling over the tinder
You gently pile the thin, dry sticks of kindling over the tinder.
> stack the logs over the kindling
You stack several layers of logs, in square fashion, over the pile of kindling.
> light a match
The match head flickers into a tiny flame.
> touch the flame to the tinder
The tinder burns quickly on contact with the flame.
> let it follow
> sing
You all begin to sing an old song together.
> add logs to the fire
The fire burns brightly for awhile, and your group tends to it, adding more logs periodically, as you continue to sing and tell stories.
> sing
As your group sings late into the night, you stop adding wood, and the flame dwindles.
sleep in tents
Your group, growing weary, crawl into their tents to sleep.
let it
follow
draw a vertical
line
Next you draw a vertical line, creating a second column.
In the second column you list the successive steps of the Voice of Fire. For each step, you draw a line between the step on the right, and the part of the story on the left to which it corresponds.
The laying of the tinder
> lay the tinder
A small patch of tinder is placed in the hearth.
The laying of the kindling over the tinder
> lay the kindling
A layer of kindling is added over the tinder.
The stacking of the firewood over the kindling
> stack the firewood
Logs of firewood are stacked systematically over the kindling.
The sparking of the tinder, creating an ember
> spark the tinder
A single spark is added to the tinder. It catches and forms an ember.
The spreading of the ember to the kindling, creating a flame
> spread to the kindling
The ember glows, spreading to the kindling above. The kindling is acquired by a growing flame.
The spreading of the flame to the firewood, creating a blaze
> spread to the firewood
The flame grows, and reaches the firewood, setting it alight. The blaze glows, feeding on the wooden fuel.
The consumption of all within the blaze
> burn
The blaze continues to spread through the logs, arranged perfectly to give themselves up to the burning. The hearth burns bright and hot, for a time.
The ash left behind
> reduce to ash
As the wooden fuel is spent, the blaze dies down, gradually dwindling to nothing. A pile of black ash is left behind in the hearth.

text.text: A group of friends takes a weekend trip to camp in the woods. (cut at top)
> speak as the friends
You speak as the friends.
> travel to the woods
You all make your way out of town, in cars piled full of food, tents and musical instruments.
You arrive at the campground in the woods.
As it darkens outside, they gather tinder, kindling and firewood.
> gather tinder, kindling and firewood
As it begins to grow dark, your group searches for and finds: - tinder - kindling - firewood
They dig a pit in the ground.
> dig a pit in the ground
You dig a pit, a foot deep and 3 feet in diameter.
They lay the tinder in the middle of the pit.
> lay the tinder in the pit
You place a patch of fluffy tinder in the pit.
They pile the kindling on over it.
> pile the kindling over the tinder
You gently pile the thin, dry sticks of kindling over the tinder.
They stack the logs in layers over the kindling.
> stack the logs over the kindling
You stack several layers of logs, in square fashion, over the pile of kindling.
One of them lights a match, and carefully touches its flame to the tinder.
> light a match
The match head flickers into a tiny flame.
> touch the flame to the tinder
The tinder burns quickly on contact with the flame.
↳ The fire starts, spreading first to the kindling and then the logs.

text.text: > speak as the friends
You speak as the friends.
> travel to the woods
You all make your way out of town, in cars piled full of food, tents and musical instruments.
You arrive at the campground in the woods.
> gather tinder, kindling and firewood
As it begins to grow dark, your group searches for and finds: - tinder - kindling - firewood
> dig a pit in the ground
You dig a pit, a foot deep and 3 feet in diameter.
> lay the tinder in the pit 1
You place a patch of fluffy tinder in the pit.
> pile the kindling over the tinder 2
You gently pile the thin, dry sticks of kindling over the tinder.
> stack the logs over the kindling
You stack several layers of logs, in square fashion, over the pile of kindling.
> light a match
The match head flickers into a tiny flame.
> touch the flame to the tinder
The tinder burns quickly on contact with the flame.
> let it follow
> sing
You all begin to sing an old song together.
> add logs to the fire
The fire burns brightly for awhile, and your group tends to it, adding more logs periodically, as you continue to sing and tell stories.

text.text: A group of friends takes a weekend trip to camp in the woods.
> speak as the friends
You speak as the friends.
> travel to the woods
You all make your way out of town, in cars piled full of food, tents and musical instruments.
You arrive at the campground in the woods.
As it darkens outside, they gather tinder, kindling and firewood.
> gather tinder, kindling and firewood
As it begins to grow dark, your group searches for and finds: - tinder - kindling - firewood
They dig a pit in the ground.
> dig a pit in the ground
You dig a pit, a foot deep and 3 feet in diameter.
They lay the tinder in the middle of the pit.
> lay the tinder in the pit 1
You place a patch of fluffy tinder in the pit.
They pile the kindling on over it.
> pile the kindling over the tinder 2
You gently pile the thin, dry sticks of kindling over the tinder.
They stack the logs in layers over the kindling.
> stack the logs over the kindling
You stack several layers of logs, in square fashion, over the pile of kindling.
One of them lights a match, and carefully touches its flame to the tinder.
> light a match
The match head flickers into a tiny flame.
touch
the flame to the tinder
The tinder burns quickly on contact with the flame.

You speak as the friends.
> travel to the woods
You all make your way out of town, in cars piled full of food, tents and musical instruments.
You arrive at the campground in the woods.
> gather tinder, kindling and firewood
As it begins to grow dark, your group searches for and finds: - tinder - kindling - firewood
> dig a pit in the ground
You dig a pit, a foot deep and 3 feet in diameter.
> lay the tinder in the pit 1 — the tinder
You place a patch of fluffy tinder in the pit.
> pile the kindling over the tinder 2 — the kindling
You gently pile the thin, dry sticks of kindling over the tinder.
> stack the logs over the kindling 3 — the firewood
You stack several layers of logs, in square fashion, over the pile of kindling.
> light a match

text.text: > listen
"Now," she says. "Consider this story:"
A group of friends takes a weekend trip to camp in the woods.
As it darkens outside, they gather tinder, kindling and firewood.
They dig a pit in the ground.
They lay the tinder in the middle of the pit.
They pile the kindling on over it.
They stack the logs in layers over the kindling.
One of them lights a match, and carefully touches its flame to the tinder.
The fire starts, spreading first to the kindling and then the logs.
The group begins to sing an old song together.
The fire burns brightly for awhile, and the friends tend to it, adding more logs periodically, as they continue to sing and tell stories.
As it grows late, they stop adding wood, and the flame dwindles. The friends retreat to their tents.
The remaining embers fizzle out, leaving behind ash.
> say that the Voice of Fire is contained in this one
"Ah, I see that the story from the Voice of Fire is contained within this one," you say.
"Indeed, my dear. Trivially so. Show it now, on the board," she says.
> pick up the chalk
She beckons you up. First you convert the story to the standard notation in a column on the left of the board:
the campfire story 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8
> say all set
"All set," you say. "Structurally nearly identical, as you said. Not quite a one-to-one mapping, but close."
"Indeed," she agrees. "Close enough for our purposes today. Now, consider another story, my dear..."

text.text: the campfire story 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8
A group of friends takes a weekend trip to camp in the woods.
> speak as the friends
You speak as the friends.
> travel to the woods
You all make your way out of town, in cars piled full of food, tents and musical instruments.
You arrive at the campground in the woods.
As it darkens outside, they gather tinder, kindling and firewood.
> gather tinder, kindling and firewood
As it begins to grow dark, your group searches for and finds: - tinder - kindling - firewood
They dig a pit in the ground.
> dig a pit in the ground
You dig a pit, a foot deep and 3 feet in diameter.
They lay the tinder in the middle of the pit.
> lay the tinder in the pit 1 — the tinder
You place a patch of fluffy tinder in the pit.
They pile the kindling on over it.
> pile the kindling over the tinder 2 — the kindling
You gently pile the thin, dry sticks of kindling over the tinder.
They stack the logs in layers over the kindling.
> stack the logs over the kindling 3 — the firewood
You stack several layers of logs, in square fashion, over the pile of kindling.
One of them lights a match, and carefully touches its flame to the tinder.
> light a match
The match head flickers into a tiny flame.
touch the flame to the tinder 4 5 6 — the ember — the flame — the blaze
The tinder burns quickly on contact with the flame.
↳ The fire starts, spreading first to the kindling and then the logs.
> let it follow
The sparking of the tinder, creating an ember (cut at top)
> spark the tinder
A single spark is added to the tinder. It catches and forms an ember.
→ the touching of the flame to the tinder
> spark the tinder — the match's flame
The tinder burns quickly on contact with the flame.
The fire starts, spreading first to the kindling and then the logs.
The spreading of the ember to the kindling, creating a flame
> spread to the kindling
The ember glows, spreading to the kindling above. The kindling is acquired by a growing flame.
→ the touching of the flame to the tinder
> spread to the kindling — the kindling, catching
The spreading of the flame to the firewood, creating a blaze
> spread to the firewood
The flame grows, and reaches the firewood, setting it alight. The blaze glows, feeding on the wooden fuel.
→ the touching of the flame to the tinder
> spread to the firewood — the logs, alight
The consumption of all within the blaze
> burn
The blaze continues to spread through the logs, arranged perfectly to give themselves up to the burning. The hearth burns bright and hot, for a time.
→ the adding of logs to the fire
> burn — the tended fire
The fire burns brightly for awhile, and your group tends to it, adding more logs periodically, as you continue to sing and tell stories.
The ash left behind
> reduce to ash
As the wooden fuel is spent, the blaze dies down, gradually dwindling to nothing. A pile of black ash is left behind in the hearth.
→ the sleeping in tents
> reduce to ash — a pile of ash
Your group, growing weary, crawl into their tents to sleep.
The remaining embers fizzle out, leaving behind ash. (cut at bottom)

text.text: They toil for weeks, chopping and laying wood over the frame, building walls and a roof. (cut at top)
Once ready, the young family moves into their new home.
Time passes.
One day, a small group of children happens upon the house while wandering through the woods.
Egging each other on, one of the children lights an oil-soaked rag on the end of a stick. He hurls it onto the roof of the house. The children scatter frantically into the woods.
The flame from the burning stick spreads to the thatch of the house's roof. Soon, the whole roof is ablaze.
The fire spreads to roof's frame, and the roof falls in.
The whole house burns to the ground, the family trapped within.
A field of ash is all that remains the next morning.
> say that it is a sad story
"Well," you say, "That's quite a sad story."
"Indeed. Can you find the Voice of Fire within it?"

"Let's see..." you say. Once again, you approach the board, converting each line of the story to the standard notation. When you reach the point where the children fling the torch onto the roof, you pause. "What is the right thing to do here? The source of the intentional voice has changed. It's no longer from the family's perspective that things are happening. It's the children's."
"Indeed," says Katya.

"Every line is spoken by someone, my dear. The one who says pack is the one who packs; the consequence is reported back to them and no one else. When the one who speaks changes, we say so above the line, and we change the ink."
She draws a short bar across the column and writes THE CHILDREN beneath it, in a second colour.

text.text: > remember the campfire story
It went like this:
> travel to the woods
You all make your way out of town, in cars piled full of food, tents and musical instruments.
You arrive at the campground in the woods.
> gather tinder, kindling and firewood
As it begins to grow dark, your group searches for and finds: - tinder - kindling - firewood
> dig a pit in the ground
You dig a pit, a foot deep and 3 feet in diameter.
> lay the tinder in the pit
You place a patch of fluffy tinder in the pit.
— the tinder
> pile the kindling over the tinder
You gently pile the thin, dry sticks of kindling over the tinder.
— the kindling
> stack the logs over the kindling
You stack several layers of logs, in square fashion, over the pile of kindling.
— the firewood
> light a match
The match head flickers into a tiny flame.
> touch the flame to the tinder
The tinder burns quickly on contact with the flame.
The fire starts, spreading first to the kindling and then the logs.
— the ember — the flame — the blaze
> sing
You all begin to sing an old song together.
> add logs to the fire
The fire burns brightly for awhile, and your group tends to it, adding more logs periodically, as you continue to sing and tell stories.
— the blaze
> sing
As your group sings late into the night, you stop adding wood, and the flame dwindles.
> sleep in tents
Your group, growing weary, crawl into their tents to sleep.
The remaining embers fizzle out, leaving behind ash.
— the ash

text.text: > lay walls and a roof
You toil for weeks, chopping and laying wood over the frame. The walls go up, and over them a roof of thatch.
Once ready, the young family moves into their new home.
> move in
Once it is ready, you move into your new home.
↳ Time passes.
> let it follow
↳ One day, a small group of children happens upon the house while wandering through the woods.
> let it follow
Egging each other on, one of the children lights an oil-soaked rag on the end of a stick. He hurls it onto the roof of the house. The children scatter frantically into the woods.
> ask what the right thing to do is

"Let's see..." you say. Once again, you approach the board, converting each line of the story to the standard notation. When you reach the point where the children fling the torch onto the roof, you pause. "What is the right thing to do here? The source of the intentional voice has changed. It's no longer from the family's perspective that things are happening. It's the children's."
"Indeed," says Katya.

"Every line is spoken by someone, my dear. The one who says pack is the one who packs; the consequence is reported back to them and no one else. When the one who speaks changes, we say so above the line, and we change the ink."
She draws a short bar across the column and writes THE CHILDREN beneath it, in a second colour.
"We do not write why they speak. We write who. Now issue their command."
She shows you how to indicate voice switches using visual notation.
YOU >
YOU speak as the children

"Let's see..." you say. Once again, you approach the board, converting each line of the story to the standard notation. When you reach the point where the children fling the torch onto the roof, you pause. "What is the right thing to do here? The source of the intentional voice has changed. It's no longer from the family's perspective that things are happening. It's the children's."
"Indeed," says Katya.

"Every line is spoken by someone, my dear. The one who says pack is the one who packs; the consequence is reported back to them and no one else. When the one who speaks changes, we say so above the line, and we change the ink."
She draws a short bar across the column and writes THE CHILDREN beneath it, in a second colour.
"We do not write why they speak. We write who. Now issue their command."
She shows you how to indicate voice switches using visual notation.

text.text: > remember the campfire story
It went like this:
> travel to the woods
You all make your way out of town, in cars piled full of food, tents and musical instruments.
You arrive at the campground in the woods.
> gather tinder, kindling and firewood
As it begins to grow dark, your group searches for and finds: - tinder - kindling - firewood
> dig a pit in the ground
You dig a pit, a foot deep and 3 feet in diameter.
> lay the tinder in the pit
You place a patch of fluffy tinder in the pit.
— the tinder
> pile the kindling over the tinder
You gently pile the thin, dry sticks of kindling over the tinder.
— the kindling
> stack the logs over the kindling
You stack several layers of logs, in square fashion, over the pile of kindling.
— the firewood
> light a match
The match head flickers into a tiny flame.
> touch the flame to the tinder
The tinder burns quickly on contact with the flame.
The fire starts, spreading first to the kindling and then the logs.
— the ember — the flame — the blaze
> sing
You all begin to sing an old song together.
> add logs to the fire
The fire burns brightly for awhile, and your group tends to it, adding more logs periodically, as you continue to sing and tell stories.

text.text: > hurl it onto the roof (cut at top)
One of you hurls the burning stick onto the roof of the house.
> scatter
You scatter frantically into the woods.
"There is no one left to speak, my dear. The children have run. Let these lines follow from what they did. We will find a voice for such things another day."
↳ The flame from the burning stick spreads to the thatch of the house's roof. Soon, the whole roof is ablaze.
> let it follow
↳ The fire spreads to roof's frame, and the roof falls in.
> let it follow
↳ The whole house burns to the ground, the family trapped within.
> let it follow
↳ A field of ash is all that remains the next morning.
> let it follow
> draw a vertical line
You complete the translation of the story. Then, as before, you add a vertical line and a new column.
A single spark is added to the tinder. It catches and forms an ember. (cut at top)
The spreading of the ember to the kindling, creating a flame
> spread to the kindling
The ember glows, spreading to the kindling above. The kindling is acquired by a growing flame.
The spreading of the flame to the firewood, creating a blaze
> spread to the firewood
The flame grows, and reaches the firewood, setting it alight. The blaze glows, feeding on the wooden fuel.
The consumption of all within the blaze
> burn
The blaze continues to spread through the logs, arranged perfectly to give themselves up to the burning. The hearth burns bright and hot, for a time.
The ash left behind
> reduce to ash
As the wooden fuel is spent, the blaze dies down, gradually dwindling to nothing. A pile of black ash is left behind in the hearth.

> map the laying of the tinder to the lighting of the rag
→ the lighting of the rag
> map the laying of the kindling to the laying of walls and a roof
→ the laying of walls and a roof
> expand the campfire story
The campfire story unfolds, above the house in the woods.

text.text: > lay walls and a roof 2
You toil for weeks, chopping and laying wood over the frame. The walls go up, and over them a roof of thatch.
Once ready, the young family moves into their new home.
> move in
Once it is ready, you move into your new home.
↳ Time passes.
> let it follow
↳ One day, a small group of children happens upon the house while wandering through the woods.
> let it follow
Egging each other on, one of the children lights an oil-soaked rag on the end of a stick. He hurls it onto the roof of the house. The children scatter frantically into the woods.
> ask what the right thing to do is

"Let's see..." you say. Once again, you approach the board, converting each line of the story to the standard notation. When you reach the point where the children fling the torch onto the roof, you pause. "What is the right thing to do here? The source of the intentional voice has changed. It's no longer from the family's perspective that things are happening. It's the children's."
"Indeed," says Katya.

"Every line is spoken by someone, my dear. The one who says pack is the one who packs; the consequence is reported back to them and no one else. When the one who speaks changes, we say so above the line, and we change the ink."
She draws a short bar across the column and writes THE CHILDREN beneath it, in a second colour.
"We do not write why they speak. We write who. Now issue their command."
She shows you how to indicate voice switches using visual notation.

text.text: > scatter 5
You scatter frantically into the woods.
"There is no one left to speak, my dear. The children have run. Let these lines follow from what they did. We will find a voice for such things another day."
↳ The flame from the burning stick spreads to the thatch of the house's roof. Soon, the whole roof is ablaze.
> let it follow
↳ The fire spreads to roof's frame, and the roof falls in.
> let it follow
↳ The whole house burns to the ground, the family trapped within.
> let it follow
↳ A field of ash is all that remains the next morning.
> let it follow
> draw a vertical line

The spreading of the ember to the kindling, creating a flame (cut at top)
> spread to the kindling
The ember glows, spreading to the kindling above. The kindling is acquired by a growing flame.
→ the scattering

> spread to the firewood
The flame grows, and reaches the firewood, setting it alight. The blaze glows, feeding on the wooden fuel.
The consumption of all within the blaze
> burn
The blaze continues to spread through the logs, arranged perfectly to give themselves up to the burning. The hearth burns bright and hot, for a time.
The ash left behind
> reduce to ash
As the wooden fuel is spent, the blaze dies down, gradually dwindling to nothing. A pile of black ash is left behind in the hearth.

text.text: "Let's see..." you say. Once again, you approach the board, converting each line of the story to the standard notation. When you reach the point where the children fling the torch onto the roof, you pause. "What is the right thing to do here? The source of the intentional voice has changed. It's no longer from the family's perspective that things are happening. It's the children's." (cut at top)
"Indeed," says Katya.

"Every line is spoken by someone, my dear. The one who says pack is the one who packs; the consequence is reported back to them and no one else. When the one who speaks changes, we say so above the line, and we change the ink."
She draws a short bar across the column and writes THE CHILDREN beneath it, in a second colour.
"We do not write why they speak. We write who. Now issue their command."
She shows you how to indicate voice switches using visual notation.
YOU > speak as the children
You speak as the children.
the children

> scatter 5 6 7 8 — the flame — the blaze — the ash
You scatter frantically into the woods.

text.text: "Let's see..." you say. Once again, you approach the board, converting each line of the story to the standard notation. When you reach the point where the children fling the torch onto the roof, you pause. "What is the right thing to do here? The source of the intentional voice has changed. It's no longer from the family's perspective that things are happening. It's the children's." (cut at top)
"Indeed," says Katya.

"Every line is spoken by someone, my dear. The one who says pack is the one who packs; the consequence is reported back to them and no one else. When the one who speaks changes, we say so above the line, and we change the ink."
She draws a short bar across the column and writes THE CHILDREN beneath it, in a second colour.
"We do not write why they speak. We write who. Now issue their command."
She shows you how to indicate voice switches using visual notation.
YOU > speak as the children
You speak as the children.
the children
> light the rag 1 — the tinder
Egging each other on, one of you lights an oil-soaked rag on the end of a stick.
> hurl it onto the roof 4 — the ember
One of you hurls the burning stick onto the roof of the house.
> scatter 5 6 7 8 — the flame — the blaze — the ash
You scatter frantically into the woods.
"There is no one left to speak, my dear. The children have run. Let these lines follow from what they did. We will find a voice for such things another day."

text.text: YOU > speak as the family
You speak as the family.
the family
> pack
You gather what you need, and leave the rest.
> travel
You depart the city together, entering the woods.
> travel
You march through the woods, making camp at night, taking shelter when the weather is bad.
> travel
You reach a clearing within the woods.
The ground here is flat and healthy.
> cut wood
You cut down the trees surrounding your clearing, and strip them of their bark.
> dig a hole
You dig into the ground in the clearing where you intend to build your home's foundation.
> build the foundation
You build a wooden foundation into the ground you have dug.
> raise the frame 3 — the firewood
Upon the foundation you raise a frame for the house that you will make.
> lay walls and a roof 2 — the kindling
You toil for weeks, chopping and laying wood over the frame. The walls go up, and over them a roof of thatch.
> move in
Once it is ready, you move into your new home.

the family

You toil for weeks, chopping and laying wood over the frame. The walls go up, and over them a roof of thatch.
↳ Time passes.
↳ One day, a small group of children happens upon the house while wandering through the woods.
Egging each other on, one of the children lights an oil-soaked rag on the end of a stick. He hurls it onto the roof of the house. The children scatter frantically into the woods.
> ask what the right thing to do is

"Let's see..." you say. Once again, you approach the board, converting each line of the story to the standard notation. When you reach the point where the children fling the torch onto the roof, you pause. "What is the right thing to do here? The source of the intentional voice has changed. It's no longer from the family's perspective that things are happening. It's the children's."
"Indeed," says Katya.

"Every line is spoken by someone, my dear. The one who says pack is the one who packs; the consequence is reported back to them and no one else. When the one who speaks changes, we say so above the line, and we change the ink."
She draws a short bar across the column and writes THE CHILDREN beneath it, in a second colour.
"We do not write why they speak. We write who. Now issue their command."
She shows you how to indicate voice switches using visual notation.

text.text: As the wooden fuel is spent, the blaze dies down, gradually dwindling to nothing. A pile of black ash is left behind in the hearth. (cut at top)
→ the scattering
> reduce to ash — a field of ash
> remember the campfire story
It went like this:
> travel to the woods
You all make your way out of town, in cars piled full of food, tents and musical instruments.
You arrive at the campground in the woods.
> gather tinder, kindling and firewood
As it begins to grow dark, your group searches for and finds: - tinder - kindling - firewood
> dig a pit in the ground
You dig a pit, a foot deep and 3 feet in diameter.
> lay the tinder in the pit
You place a patch of fluffy tinder in the pit.
— the tinder
> pile the kindling over the tinder
You gently pile the thin, dry sticks of kindling over the tinder.
— the kindling
> stack the logs over the kindling
You stack several layers of logs, in square fashion, over the pile of kindling.
— the firewood
> light a match
The match head flickers into a tiny flame.
> touch the flame to the tinder
The tinder burns quickly on contact with the flame.
The fire starts, spreading first to the kindling and then the logs.
— the ember — the flame — the blaze
> sing
You all begin to sing an old song together.
> add logs to the fire
The fire burns brightly for awhile, and your group tends to it, adding more logs periodically, as you continue to sing and tell stories.

text.text: > raise the frame 3
Upon the foundation you raise a frame for the house that you will make.
They toil for weeks, chopping and laying wood over the frame, building walls and a roof.
> lay walls and a roof 2
You toil for weeks, chopping and laying wood over the frame. The walls go up, and over them a roof of thatch.
Once ready, the young family moves into their new home.
> move in
Once it is ready, you move into your new home.
↳ Time passes.
> let it follow
↳ One day, a small group of children happens upon the house while wandering through the woods.
> let it follow
Egging each other on, one of the children lights an oil-soaked rag on the end of a stick. He hurls it onto the roof of the house. The children scatter frantically into the woods.
> ask what the right thing to do is

"Let's see..." you say. Once again, you approach the board, converting each line of the story to the standard notation. When you reach the point where the children fling the torch onto the roof, you pause. "What is the right thing to do here? The source of the intentional voice has changed. It's no longer from the family's perspective that things are happening. It's the children's."
"Indeed," says Katya.

"Every line is spoken by someone, my dear. The one who says pack is the one who packs; the consequence is reported back to them and no one else. When the one who speaks changes, we say so above the line, and we change the ink."

Upon the foundation you raise a frame for the house that you will make.
They toil for weeks, chopping and laying wood over the frame, building walls and a roof.
> lay walls and a roof 2
You toil for weeks, chopping and laying wood over the frame. The walls go up, and over them a roof of thatch.
Once ready, the young family moves into their new home.
> move in
Once it is ready, you move into your new home.
↳ Time passes.
> let it follow
↳ One day, a small group of children happens upon the house while wandering through the woods.
> let it follow
Egging each other on, one of the children lights an oil-soaked rag on the end of a stick. He hurls it onto the roof of the house. The children scatter frantically into the woods.
> ask what the right thing to do is

"Let's see..." you say. Once again, you approach the board, converting each line of the story to the standard notation. When you reach the point where the children fling the torch onto the roof, you pause. "What is the right thing to do here? The source of the intentional voice has changed. It's no longer from the family's perspective that things are happening. It's the children's."
"Indeed," says Katya.

"Every line is spoken by someone, my dear. The one who says pack is the one who packs; the consequence is reported back to them and no one else. When the one who speaks changes, we say so above the line, and we change the ink."

text.text: YOU > speak as the family
You speak as the family.
the family
They build a wooden foundation into the ground, and upon this structure a frame for the house that they will make.
> raise the frame 3
Upon the foundation you raise a frame for the house that you will make.
They toil for weeks, chopping and laying wood over the frame, building walls and a roof.
> lay walls and a roof 2
You toil for weeks, chopping and laying wood over the frame. The walls go up, and over them a roof of thatch.
↳ Time passes.
↳ One day, a small group of children happens upon the house while wandering through the woods.
Egging each other on, one of the children lights an oil-soaked rag on the end of a stick. He hurls it onto the roof of the house. The children scatter frantically into the woods.
> ask what the right thing to do is

"Let's see..." you say. Once again, you approach the board, converting each line of the story to the standard notation. When you reach the point where the children fling the torch onto the roof, you pause. "What is the right thing to do here? The source of the intentional voice has changed. It's no longer from the family's perspective that things are happening. It's the children's."
"Indeed," says Katya.

text.text: > build the foundation 3
You build a wooden foundation into the ground you have dug.
They toil for weeks, chopping and laying wood over the frame, building walls and a roof.
> lay walls and a roof 2
You toil for weeks, chopping and laying wood over the frame. The walls go up, and over them a roof of thatch.
↳ Time passes.
↳ One day, a small group of children happens upon the house while wandering through the woods.
Egging each other on, one of the children lights an oil-soaked rag on the end of a stick. He hurls it onto the roof of the house. The children scatter frantically into the woods.
> ask what the right thing to do is

"Let's see..." you say. Once again, you approach the board, converting each line of the story to the standard notation. When you reach the point where the children fling the torch onto the roof, you pause. "What is the right thing to do here? The source of the intentional voice has changed. It's no longer from the family's perspective that things are happening. It's the children's."
"Indeed," says Katya.

"Every line is spoken by someone, my dear. The one who says pack is the one who packs; the consequence is reported back to them and no one else. When the one who speaks changes, we say so above the line, and we change the ink."
She draws a short bar across the column and writes THE CHILDREN beneath it, in a second colour.
"We do not write why they speak. We write who. Now issue their command."
She shows you how to indicate voice switches using visual notation.

text.text: > scatter (cut at top)
You scatter frantically into the woods.
The flame from the burning stick spreads to the thatch of the house's roof. Soon, the whole roof is ablaze.
The fire spreads to roof's frame, and the roof falls in.
The whole house burns to the ground, the family trapped within.
A field of ash is all that remains the next morning.
— the flame — the blaze — the ash
It felt like the flame, and the blaze, and the ash, in the Voice of Fire.

text.text: > listen
A young family moves out of the city.
After some travel, they find a clearing in the woods, away from everything and everyone they've ever known.
They begin to cut the trees in the surrounding wood. They begin to dig into the ground in the clearing.
They build a wooden foundation into the ground, and upon this structure a frame for the house that they will make.
They toil for weeks, chopping and laying wood over the frame, building walls and a roof.
Once ready, the young family moves into their new home.
Time passes.
One day, a small group of children happens upon the house while wandering through the woods.
Egging each other on, one of the children lights an oil-soaked rag on the end of a stick. He hurls it onto the roof of the house. The children scatter frantically into the woods.
The flame from the burning stick spreads to the thatch of the house's roof. Soon, the whole roof is ablaze.
The fire spreads to roof's frame, and the roof falls in.
The whole house burns to the ground, the family trapped within.
A field of ash is all that remains the next morning.
> say that it is a sad story
"Well," you say, "That's quite a sad story."
"Indeed. Can you find the Voice of Fire within it?"

The house in the woods goes up on the board.

text.text: > listen (cut at top)
A seed takes root in fertile ground.
The season is right, and the weather is right, and a sapling rises forth.
It grows, and time passes, and the weather is right, and it lives to become a tree.
The tree sprouts leaves and seeds, and the season changes, and the seeds fall to the ground and the leaves protect them.
Gradually, more trees sprout and grow and spread.
Much time passes. The trees flourish, a forest.
The weather becomes dry and hot, and the forest suffers. Many trees die and the ground is covered in dead brush.
The weather happens to bring a thunderstorm. A lightning bolt strikes a dead tree, and it begins to burn.
The flame spreads to the dead brush on the ground, and out to more trees.
The fire burns in a rapidly-growing circle around the lightning strike.
The forest is consumed in fire. Trees and brush are burnt to the ground.
The flame stops at rivers and sand and rocks. The forest burns down to ash.
> pick up the chalk
The forest fire goes up on the board.
the forest fire
A seed takes root in fertile ground.
YOU > speak as the seed
You speak as the seed.
"Who takes root, my dear? No one, you would say. The notation has no line for no one. Something must command the seed, or the seed cannot be written."
She writes THE SEED above the line, in a colour you have not seen her use, with a broken bar.
"When nothing wants a thing, we lend it a voice anyway. The seed's. The weather's. The fire's. A voice without a body and without a wish."

text.text: the forest fire (cut at top)
A seed takes root in fertile ground.
YOU > speak as the seed
You speak as the seed.
"Who takes root, my dear? No one, you would say. The notation has no line for no one. Something must command the seed, or the seed cannot be written."
She writes THE SEED above the line, in a colour you have not seen her use, with a broken bar.
"When nothing wants a thing, we lend it a voice anyway. The seed's. The weather's. The fire's. A voice without a body and without a wish."
the seed
> take root
The seed takes root in fertile ground.
The season is right, and the weather is right, and a sapling rises forth.
YOU > speak as the season
You speak as the season.
"The season is right, my dear. Time passes. Those are voices too, of a thinner kind. The season commands; time commands. They have no body and no place. Write them with a double bar."
Katya teaches you about disembodied and abstract voices in the standard notation.
the season
> turn
The season turns. The weather is right, and a sapling rises forth.
It grows, and time passes, and the weather is right, and it lives to become a tree.
YOU > speak as the tree
You speak as the tree.
the tree
grow

text.text: > turn dry and hot
The weather becomes dry and hot, and the forest suffers. Many trees die. The forest stands full of dead trees, and the ground is covered in dead brush.
The weather happens to bring a thunderstorm. A lightning bolt strikes a dead tree, and it begins to burn.
> bring a thunderstorm
A thunderstorm comes over the forest. A lightning bolt strikes a dead tree, and it begins to burn.
The flame spreads to the dead brush on the ground, and out to more trees.
YOU > speak as the fire
You speak as the fire.
the fire
> spread to the dead brush
The flame spreads to the dead brush on the ground, and out to more trees.
The fire burns in a rapidly-growing circle around the lightning strike.
> burn in a growing circle
The fire burns in a rapidly-growing circle around the lightning strike.
The forest is consumed in fire. Trees and brush are burnt to the ground.
> consume the forest
The forest is consumed in fire. Trees and brush are burnt to the ground.
The flame stops at rivers and sand and rocks. The forest burns down to ash.
> stop at the rivers
The flame stops at rivers and sand and rocks. The forest burns down to ash.
> draw a vertical line
You repeat the exercise.
> lay the kindling
A layer of kindling is added over the tinder.
The stacking of the firewood over the kindling
> stack the firewood
Logs of firewood are stacked systematically over the kindling.
The sparking of the tinder, creating an ember
> spark the tinder
A single spark is added to the tinder. It catches and forms an ember.
The spreading of the ember to the kindling, creating a flame
> spread to the kindling
The ember glows, spreading to the kindling above. The kindling is acquired by a growing flame.
The spreading of the flame to the firewood, creating a blaze
> spread to the firewood
The flame grows, and reaches the firewood, setting it alight. The blaze glows, feeding on the wooden fuel.
The consumption of all within the blaze
> burn
The blaze continues to spread through the logs, arranged perfectly to give themselves up to the burning. The hearth burns bright and hot, for a time.
The ash left behind
> reduce to ash
As the wooden fuel is spent, the blaze dies down, gradually dwindling to nothing. A pile of black ash is left behind in the hearth.

text.text: — the flame — the blaze — the ash (cut at top)
It felt:
— sad, because it was a home
— a bit cold, because the pattern did not mind
— unfinished, because the tinder is still two things
— like the Voice of Fire, because the tinder was the thatch, and before that the oil-soaked rag
> listen
A seed takes root in fertile ground.
The season is right, and the weather is right, and a sapling rises forth.
It grows, and time passes, and the weather is right, and it lives to become a tree.
The tree sprouts leaves and seeds, and the season changes, and the seeds fall to the ground and the leaves protect them.
Gradually, more trees sprout and grow and spread.
Much time passes. The trees flourish, a forest.
The weather becomes dry and hot, and the forest suffers. Many trees die and the ground is covered in dead brush.
The weather happens to bring a thunderstorm. A lightning bolt strikes a dead tree, and it begins to burn.
The flame spreads to the dead brush on the ground, and out to more trees.
The fire burns in a rapidly-growing circle around the lightning strike.
The forest is consumed in fire. Trees and brush are burnt to the ground.
The flame stops at rivers and sand and rocks. The forest burns down to ash.
> pick up the chalk
The forest fire goes up on the board.

"And now, the final story for today's lesson," says Katya...

text.text: Some of his followers begin to write down the wise man's teachings.
The man dies unexpectedly.
His closest followers construct a great funeral pyre, and lay his body on it.
The wise man's funeral is attended by multitudes of his followers.

The pyre is lit. The flame spreads from tinder to kindling to wood, and consumes the dead man's body. His followers weep and cry out and sing. Eventually, the flame is gone. The wise man's body is reduced to ash.

The most central followers continue to write the dead man's words, and in time they adjust his words, and embellish the stories about him, in the interest of reaching as many people as possible. His death becomes mythologized.
Books spread across the land. The words that are distorted echoes of the wise man's ideas are read and repeated and reprinted.
Time passes. The words are interpretted and reinterpretted until they hardly resemble the original ideas at all.
> pick up the chalk
The wise man's story goes up on the board.

As a man, he seeks answers to old questions. Questions of purpose, consciousness, the dynamics of reality.

> light the pyre

> lay the kindling

> stack the firewood
Logs of firewood are stacked systematically over the kindling.
The sparking of the tinder, creating an ember
> spark the tinder
A single spark is added to the tinder. It catches and forms an ember.
The spreading of the ember to the kindling, creating a flame
> spread to the kindling

> spread to the firewood
The flame grows, and reaches the firewood, setting it alight. The blaze glows, feeding on the wooden fuel.
The consumption of all within the blaze
> burn

> reduce to ash
As the wooden fuel is spent, the blaze dies down, gradually dwindling to nothing. A pile of black ash is left behind in the hearth.

> lay the tinder
A small patch of tinder is placed in the hearth.
The laying of the kindling over the tinder
> lay the kindling
A layer of kindling is added over the tinder.
The stacking of the firewood over the kindling
> stack the firewood
Logs of firewood are stacked systematically over the kindling.
The sparking of the tinder, creating an ember
> spark the tinder
A single spark is added to the tinder. It catches and forms an ember.
The spreading of the ember to the kindling, creating a flame
> spread to the kindling
The ember glows, spreading to the kindling above. The kindling is acquired by a growing flame.
The spreading of the flame to the firewood, creating a blaze
> spread to the firewood
The flame grows, and reaches the firewood, setting it alight. The blaze glows, feeding on the wooden fuel.
The consumption of all within the blaze
> burn

text.text: > remember the campfire story
It went like this:
> travel to the woods
You all make your way out of town, in cars piled full of food, tents and musical instruments.
You arrive at the campground in the woods.
> gather tinder, kindling and firewood
As it begins to grow dark, your group searches for and finds: - tinder - kindling - firewood
> dig a pit in the ground
You dig a pit, a foot deep and 3 feet in diameter.
> lay the tinder in the pit
You place a patch of fluffy tinder in the pit.
— the tinder
> pile the kindling over the tinder
You gently pile the thin, dry sticks of kindling over the tinder.
— the kindling
> stack the logs over the kindling
You stack several layers of logs, in square fashion, over the pile of kindling.
— the firewood
> light a match
The match head flickers into a tiny flame.
> touch the flame to the tinder
The tinder burns quickly on contact with the flame.
The fire starts, spreading first to the kindling and then the logs.
— the ember — the flame — the blaze
> sing
You all begin to sing an old song together.
> add logs to the fire
The fire burns brightly for awhile, and your group tends to it, adding more logs periodically, as you continue to sing and tell stories.
— the blaze

text.text: The pyre is lit. The flame spreads from tinder to kindling to wood, and consumes the dead man's body. His followers weep and cry out and sing. Eventually, the flame is gone. The wise man's body is reduced to ash. (cut at top)

The most central followers continue to write the dead man's words, and in time they adjust his words, and embellish the stories about him, in the interest of reaching as many people as possible. His death becomes mythologized.
> adjust and embellish his words

→ the constructing of the pyre

→ the constructing of the pyre

The spreading of the ember to the kindling, creating a flame

The spreading of the flame to the firewood, creating a blaze
> spread to the firewood

text.text: > remember the campfire story
It went like this:
> travel to the woods
You all make your way out of town, in cars piled full of food, tents and musical instruments.
You arrive at the campground in the woods.
> gather tinder, kindling and firewood
As it begins to grow dark, your group searches for and finds: - tinder - kindling - firewood
> dig a pit in the ground
You dig a pit, a foot deep and 3 feet in diameter.
> lay the tinder in the pit
You place a patch of fluffy tinder in the pit.
— the tinder
> pile the kindling over the tinder
You gently pile the thin, dry sticks of kindling over the tinder.
— the kindling
> stack the logs over the kindling
You stack several layers of logs, in square fashion, over the pile of kindling.
— the firewood
> light a match
The match head flickers into a tiny flame.
> touch the flame to the tinder
The tinder burns quickly on contact with the flame.
The fire starts, spreading first to the kindling and then the logs.
— the ember — the flame — the blaze
> sing
You all begin to sing an old song together.
> add logs to the fire
The fire burns brightly for awhile, and your group tends to it, adding more logs periodically, as you continue to sing and tell stories.

The pyre is lit. The flame spreads from tinder to kindling to wood, and consumes the dead man's body. His followers weep and cry out and sing. Eventually, the flame is gone. The wise man's body is reduced to ash.

the closest followers
> light the pyre 4

The pyre is lit. The flame spreads from tinder to kindling to wood, and consumes the dead man's body. His followers weep and cry out and sing. Eventually, the flame is gone. The wise man's body is reduced to ash.

> lay the tinder

> lay the kindling

→ the constructing of the pyre
The stacking of the firewood over the kindling
> stack the firewood
Logs of firewood are stacked systematically over the kindling.
→ the constructing of the pyre
The sparking of the tinder, creating an ember
> spark the tinder
A single spark is added to the tinder. It catches and forms an ember.
→ the lighting of the pyre
The spreading of the ember to the kindling, creating a flame
> spread to the kindling
The ember glows, spreading to the kindling above. The kindling is acquired by a growing flame.
The spreading of the flame to the firewood, creating a blaze
> spread to the firewood
The flame grows, and reaches the firewood, setting it alight. The blaze glows, feeding on the wooden fuel.
The consumption of all within the blaze
> burn
The blaze continues to spread through the logs, arranged perfectly to give themselves up to the burning. The hearth burns bright and hot, for a time.

text.text: You speak as the closest followers. (cut at top)
the closest followers
> light the pyre 4 5 6 7 8 — the ember — the flame — the blaze — the ash

The pyre is lit. The flame spreads from tinder to kindling to wood, and consumes the dead man's body. His followers weep and cry out and sing. Eventually, the flame is gone. The wise man's body is reduced to ash.

The most central followers continue to write the dead man's words, and in time they adjust his words, and embellish the stories about him, in the interest of reaching as many people as possible. His death becomes mythologized.

text.text: You speak as the man. (cut at bottom)
The laying of the tinder
> lay the tinder
A small patch of tinder is placed in the hearth.
→ the constructing of the pyre
> lay the tinder — the pyre's tinder
You construct a great funeral pyre, and lay his body on it.
The laying of the kindling over the tinder
> lay the kindling
A layer of kindling is added over the tinder.
→ the constructing of the pyre
> lay the kindling — the pyre's kindling
The stacking of the firewood over the kindling
> stack the firewood
Logs of firewood are stacked systematically over the kindling.
→ the constructing of the pyre
> stack the firewood — the pyre's wood
The sparking of the tinder, creating an ember
> spark the tinder
A single spark is added to the tinder. It catches and forms an ember.
→ the lighting of the pyre
> spark the tinder — the flame

The pyre is lit. The flame spreads from tinder to kindling to wood, and consumes the dead man's body. His followers weep and cry out and sing. Eventually, the flame is gone. The wise man's body is reduced to ash.

text.text: > remember the campfire story
It went like this:
> travel to the woods
You all make your way out of town, in cars piled full of food, tents and musical instruments.
You arrive at the campground in the woods.
> gather tinder, kindling and firewood
As it begins to grow dark, your group searches for and finds: - tinder - kindling - firewood
> dig a pit in the ground
You dig a pit, a foot deep and 3 feet in diameter.
> lay the tinder in the pit
You place a patch of fluffy tinder in the pit.
— the tinder
> pile the kindling over the tinder
You gently pile the thin, dry sticks of kindling over the tinder.
— the kindling
> stack the logs over the kindling
You stack several layers of logs, in square fashion, over the pile of kindling.
— the firewood
> light a match
The match head flickers into a tiny flame.
> touch the flame to the tinder
The tinder burns quickly on contact with the flame.
The fire starts, spreading first to the kindling and then the logs.
— the ember — the flame — the blaze
> sing
You all begin to sing an old song together.
> add logs to the fire
The fire burns brightly for awhile, and your group tends to it, adding more logs periodically, as you continue to sing and tell stories.
— the blaze

text.text: > sing
As your group sings late into the night, you stop adding wood, and the flame dwindles.
> sleep in tents
Your group, growing weary, crawl into their tents to sleep.
The remaining embers fizzle out, leaving behind ash.
— the ash
It felt:

The construction of the fireplace is the replication of the man's wisdom within his mind (tinder), his initial and central followers (kindling), and the wider community of followers (firewood). It takes you some time, but you gradually work it out. The construction of the fireplace is the replication of the man's wisdom within his mind (tinder), his initial and central followers (kindling), and the wider community of followers (firewood). The mythologizing of his death marks the spark, which yields ever increasing distortions to his ideology, which spread through his original community and beyond. At the end, his wisdom has become ash, spread far and wide across the adherents to the book.

text.text: > remember the wise man's story
It went like this:
> be born
You are born to parents of no consequence.
> grow up and acquire wisdom
You are curious, charismatic, intelligent. You grow up and acquire wisdom.
— the tinder
> seek answers to old questions
You seek answers to old questions. Questions of purpose, consciousness, the dynamics of reality.
> gain a small circle of seekers
You gain a small circle of like-minded seekers who listen to you, astounded by your ideas.
— the kindling
> grow in number
You grow in number. Word of the man's wisdom spreads, and more of you come.
— the firewood
> give speeches
You give speeches to more and more devoted followers. You begin to repeat yourself. Your words become ear-worms, ever more viral and convincing.
> write down his teachings
Some of you begin to write down the wise man's teachings.
> die unexpectedly
You die unexpectedly.
> construct a pyre and lay his body on it
You construct a great funeral pyre, and lay his body on it.
> attend the funeral
You attend the wise man's funeral in multitudes.
> light the pyre

The pyre is lit. The flame spreads from tinder to kindling to wood, and consumes the dead man's body. His followers weep and cry out and sing. Eventually, the flame is gone. The wise man's body is reduced to ash.

— the ember
— the flame
> spread across the land
Books spread across the land.

text.text: > remember the wise man's story
It went like this:
> be born
You are born to parents of no consequence.
> grow up and acquire wisdom
You are curious, charismatic, intelligent. You grow up and acquire wisdom.
— the tinder
> seek answers to old questions
You seek answers to old questions. Questions of purpose, consciousness, the dynamics of reality.
> gain a small circle of seekers
You gain a small circle of like-minded seekers who listen to you, astounded by your ideas.
— the kindling
> grow in number
You grow in number. Word of the man's wisdom spreads, and more of you come.
— the firewood
> give speeches
You give speeches to more and more devoted followers. You begin to repeat yourself. Your words become ear-worms, ever more viral and convincing.
> write down his teachings
Some of you begin to write down the wise man's teachings.
> die unexpectedly
You die unexpectedly.
> construct a pyre and lay his body on it
You construct a great funeral pyre, and lay his body on it.
> attend the funeral
You attend the wise man's funeral in multitudes.
> light the pyre

The pyre is lit. The flame spreads from tinder to kindling to wood, and consumes the dead man's body. His followers weep and cry out and sing. Eventually, the flame is gone. The wise man's body is reduced to ash.
> adjust and embellish his words

You continue to write the dead man's words, and in time you adjust his words, and embellish the stories about him, in the interest of reaching as many people as possible. His death becomes mythologized.
— the ember
— the flame
> spread across the land
Books spread across the land.
— the blaze
> be read and repeated and reprinted

text.text: — the blaze
> be read and repeated and reprinted
The words that are distorted echoes of the wise man's ideas are read and repeated and reprinted.
— the blaze
> pass
Time passes. The words are interpreted and reinterpreted until they hardly resemble the original ideas at all.
— the ash
It felt:
— a bit relieving, at first, because only two lines burned
— then not, because all of them did
— unconvincing, because you don't really see it
— like the Voice of Fire, because the tinder was his wisdom
> remember the saying of Ok, I guess
It went like this:
> say Ok, I guess
"Ok, I guess," you mutter.
But you don't really see it.
It felt a bit untrue, because it was.
> remember the second picking up of the chalk
It went like this:
> pick up the chalk
The house in the woods goes up on the board.
It felt a bit ordinary, because it was chalk.
> remember the ember

The ember has been: the match's flame, in the campfire story; the burning stick, in the house in the woods, set aside; the lit rag, in the house in the woods; the lightning, in the forest fire; the flame, in the wise man's story, set aside; the myth of his death, in the wise man's story.

text.text: the house in the woods 3 2 1 4 5 6 7 8
A young family moves out of the city.
YOU > speak as the family
You speak as the family.
the family
> pack
You gather what you need, and leave the rest.
> travel
You depart the city together, entering the woods.
After some travel, they find a clearing in the woods, away from everything and everyone they've ever known.
> travel
You march through the woods, making camp at night, taking shelter when the weather is bad.
> travel
You reach a clearing within the woods.
The ground here is flat and healthy.
They begin to cut the trees in the surrounding wood. They begin to dig into the ground in the clearing.
> cut wood
You cut down the trees surrounding your clearing, and strip them of their bark.

You toil for weeks, chopping and laying wood over the frame. The walls go up, and over them a roof of thatch.

text.text: > move in 1
Once it is ready, you move into your new home.
↳ Time passes.
> let it follow
↳ One day, a small group of children happens upon the house while wandering through the woods.
> let it follow
Egging each other on, one of the children lights an oil-soaked rag on the end of a stick. He hurls it onto the roof of the house. The children scatter frantically into the woods.
> ask what the right thing to do is

"Let's see..." you say. Once again, you approach the board, converting each line of the story to the standard notation. When you reach the point where the children fling the torch onto the roof, you pause. "What is the right thing to do here? The source of the intentional voice has changed. It's no longer from the family's perspective that things are happening. It's the children's."
"Indeed," says Katya.

"Every line is spoken by someone, my dear. The one who says pack is the one who packs; the consequence is reported back to them and no one else. When the one who speaks changes, we say so above the line, and we change the ink."

You toil for weeks, chopping and laying wood over the frame. The walls go up, and over them a roof of thatch.

Upon the foundation you raise a frame for the house that you will make.

text.text: > expand the unmapped
The unmapped rows unfold.
> apply the Voice of Fire
> remember the tinder
The tinder has been: a patch of tinder, in the campfire story; the oil-soaked rag, in the house in the woods, set aside; the thatch, in the house in the woods.
> object that there is no clear tinder

"Quite a bit different, this time," you mutter. "There's not a clear answer for what's tinder, or kindling, or firewood. Is the tinder the oil-soaked rag, or the thatch on the roof? And in this case, the so-called 'fireplace' wasn't purposefully built up to be burnt; it was a family's home. The burning was done by someone else."

"Quite right," says Katya. "But these details are not relevant from the perspective of the Voice of Fire, my dear. It knows only of the preparation of the fuel, and the burning of the fuel. It knows nothing of the purposes or intentions behind these actions. It simply proceeds. A pattern."
> say that it knows nothing of the morality of the burning either
"And it seems to know nothing of the morality of the burning, either," you say.
"Indeed not," she says.
> put down the chalk
Katya continues the lesson with another story...
> map the living in their home to the moving in
→ the moving in
> map the entering of their home to the lighting of the rag
They came upon it. Did they go in?
> map the taking of things from their home to the hurling of the rag onto the roof
What did they take?
"Not every voice fits every story, my dear. That is a lesson for another day."

text.text: It felt:
— a bit relieving, at first, because only two lines burned
— then not, because all of them did
— unconvincing, because you don't really see it
— like the Voice of Fire, because the tinder was his wisdom
> remember the saying of Ok, I guess
It went like this:
> say Ok, I guess
"Ok, I guess," you mutter.
But you don't really see it.
It felt a bit untrue, because it was.
> remember the second picking up of the chalk
It went like this:
> pick up the chalk
The house in the woods goes up on the board.
It felt a bit ordinary, because it was chalk.
> remember the ember

The ember has been: the match's flame, in the campfire story; the burning stick, in the house in the woods, set aside; the lit rag, in the house in the woods; the lightning, in the forest fire; the flame, in the wise man's story, set aside; the myth of his death, in the wise man's story.
> remember the lighting of the pyre
It went like this:
> light the pyre

The pyre is lit. The flame spreads from tinder to kindling to wood, and consumes the dead man's body. His followers weep and cry out and sing. Eventually, the flame is gone. The wise man's body is reduced to ash.
It felt like the ember, and the flame, and the blaze, and the ash, in the Voice of Fire; set aside.
> try the Pillaging on the house in the woods
The house in the woods comes back up, with the Pillaging's steps beside the Fire's.
